hook.text: Sooner or later, the interviewer stops asking for code. They hand you a number and ask what it means, and then how you'd explain it to someone who has never written a query. There are fourteen questions to be ready for.

plan.text: Ten of them hide a trap, so we'll take those slowly. The other four get one answer each, in a rapid-fire round.

median-in.text: The first is about the number every report leads with.

median.text: Question one. When would you report the median instead of the mean?

median-skew.text: When the data is skewed. Here are five hundred orders. Most are small, and a long tail runs out past a hundred dollars.

median-pull.text: The median order is twenty-three eleven. The mean is twenty-six fifty-eight, dragged to the right by the tail. Only a hundred and eighty-one of the five hundred orders are above it.

median-both.text: Income, house prices and session lengths all look like this. Report the median as the typical value, and both when the gap between them is the story.

corr-in.text: Next, two numbers that move together.

corr.text: Question two. Explain correlation does not imply causation, with an example.

corr-ice.text: Two hundred days. On days when more ice cream sells, more people drown. The correlation is point five seven.

corr-heat.text: Ice cream doesn't cause drowning. Hot weather drives both: more people buy ice cream, and more people swim. The hot days sit together, top right. Temperature is the confounder.

corr-fixed.text: Hold temperature fixed, and the link all but vanishes: point zero eight. To argue a cause, you need an experiment, like an A B test, where random groups see version A or version B, or a careful causal design.

coef.text: Question three. What's the difference between correlation and the correlation coefficient?

coef-r.text: Correlation is the idea: two things moving together. The coefficient is a number for it. Pearson's r measures how close the points lie to a straight line, from minus one to one.

coef-u.text: So it can miss a pattern you can see. A perfect U scores zero.

coef-curve.text: And a curve that only ever rises scores point eight one. Spearman ranks the values first, and gives it a perfect one. Use it when the relationship is monotonic but not straight, or when the data is ordinal.

bias-in.text: Then, where the data came from.

bias.text: Question four. What is sampling bias, and how can it distort results?

bias-who.text: Say you survey your app's users about how happy they are. You've left out everyone who already left: here, nearly a quarter of them, and the unhappiest. That's survivorship bias. A web poll that only hears from the keenest is self-selection.

bias-truth.text: Across all hundred thousand users, the average score is five point nine eight. Among the ones who stayed, it's six point five six.

bias-bigger.text: Survey twenty of them, thirty times over, and the answers scatter. Survey two thousand, and they settle, on six point five six. A bigger sample shrinks the noise. It does nothing about the bias. The fix is the design: a random or stratified sample of everyone.

metric-in.text: The next one is the classic open question.

metric.text: Question five. A metric went up twenty percent week over week. How do you investigate?

metric-steps.text: State your assumptions, then take it apart. Is it real, or a tracking change, bot traffic, or a deploy? Which region, platform or cohort moved? Is it the day of the week, or the season?

metric-denom.text: And did the denominator move? Here, conversion went from three percent to three point six: up twenty percent. But orders fell four percent. Sessions fell twenty. The rate rose because the traffic dropped.

metric-end.text: Finish with the most likely driver, and what you'd check next.

quantile-in.text: Two questions about the edges of the data.

quantile.text: Question six. What are percentiles and quartiles?

quantile-def.text: A percentile is a cut. The ninetieth percentile is the value with about ninety percent of the data at or below it. Quartiles cut at twenty-five, fifty and seventy-five.

quantile-cuts.text: Here are thirteen amounts, in order. The first quartile, Q one, is ten. The median is twelve, and the third quartile, Q three, is thirteen. Between them is the interquartile range, the IQR: three.

quantile-p90.text: The ninetieth percentile is a hundred fifty-four point eight, an amount nobody spent. Pandas interpolates between fourteen and one ninety. Other tools use other rules, so exact answers can differ.

outlier.text: Question seven. How do you identify outliers?

outlier-iqr.text: The IQR rule puts a fence one and a half IQRs past each quartile: here, at five and a half and seventeen and a half. Two hundred and one ninety are outside.

outlier-z.text: A z-score counts standard deviations from the mean. But those two drag the mean up to thirty-nine and a half, and the standard deviation to sixty-nine. So two hundred is only two point three two out.

outlier-mask.text: With a cutoff of two, both are caught. With three, nothing is: the outliers hide themselves.

outlier-look.text: Either way, look before you delete. An outlier can be a typo, or the most important row you have.

present-in.text: The last three are about saying it out loud.

present.text: Question eight. How do you present a finding to a non-technical stakeholder?

present-lead.text: Lead with the answer and what it means for the business, not the method. Put the takeaway in the title, and show one clear chart rather than a table.

present-close.text: Say the caveats plainly, like this excludes refunds. End with what you recommend. The method goes in the appendix.

plain.text: Question nine. How do you explain a complex statistical finding in plain language? Anchor it to one number people can picture: customers who saw the new design were twelve percent more likely to buy.

plain-jargon.text: Drop the jargon. Instead of a ninety-five percent confidence interval, say we're highly confident the true lift is between eight and sixteen percent. Then tie it to the decision it informs.

uncertain.text: Question ten. How do you communicate uncertainty? Say what the number rests on, like the last ninety days. Give a range, not just a point. Name the assumptions, and how far the answer moves if they're wrong.

uncertain-precise.text: And don't be falsely precise. Twelve point three seven percent is about twelve, when the range runs from eight to sixteen.

rapid-in.text: That's the ten traps. Now, four questions, one answer each.

r-var.text: Variance is the average squared distance from the mean. Standard deviation is its square root, back in the data's own units. Ten to fifty gives two fifty and fifteen point eight one. Pandas divides by n minus one.

r-mode.text: The mode is the most common value, and the center that works for categories: the most common ticket is billing. Two modes are a reason to split the data.

r-normal.text: A normal distribution is a symmetric bell, set by its mean and standard deviation. Sixty-eight percent falls within one standard deviation, ninety-five within two, ninety-nine point seven within three.

r-pop.text: And the population is everyone you care about. A sample is the part you measured, and its mean is only an estimate. Three samples of fifty give fifty-two point one, fifty-one point eight and fifty-one point one. The population's mean is fifty point two.
